title: Understanding CSS random()
partialText:
One develops a certain degree of muscle memory putting together an in-depth course on JavaScript's arcane workings. That's why a particularly keen-eyed reader might notice that the posts on my own blog have started shamelessly copying taking inspiration from features that you'll see here on Piccalilli.

These little margin notes, for example.

In the earliest drafts of JavaScript for Everyone I was using Piccalilli's <SideNote> component to solve for a specific problem that I ran into almost immediately: JavaScript is made out of JavaScript, and you can't cover almost any topic or syntax without touching on dozens of other topics and syntaxes. When I found myself backed into a corner by terminology and concepts related to the topic at hand that we hadn't yet covered, I would use a side note to call it out — a way to keep from littering every lesson's prose with "which we'll cover later"s and "don't worry about this yet"s:

As tends to happen with any feature, the more I found myself settling into the project, the looser the use case for these little components became:

...And owing to a condition that I call The Speedrunner's Temperament, I inevitably ended up using them to play with the boundaries of the medium a little bit, just to see what I could get away with:

I ended up really missing these little widgets when I'd be writing for my own site, so I used a little bit of my downtime this week to steal take inspiration from them. The core of it ends up bring a relatively light lift, thanks to grid layout and a quick Eleventy shortcode that parses a supplied string as Markdown and returns the result wrapped in <aside class="sidenote"></aside>. I use "hand-scribbled" accents for notation on my website, so I carried that sort of design treatment over to these as well:

Good start, but anything worth doing is worth doing to ludicrous excess, I always say: a subtle application of animation-timeline: view() makes them fade in and scale up ever-so-slightly as they approached the center of the viewport, by a slightly different scale() factor across breakpoints. That had things looking pretty sharp, but arguably a little too sharp — these were meant to be "scribbled in the margins" both tonally and in terms of presentation, and a perfectly squared span of text wasn't quite getting that across. Easy enough to put a quick transform: rotate(2deg) on there too, but that would still give me a uniform result throughout the page:

What I needed was some old fashioned, organic-style jank, and that gave me the perfect excuse to finally try out the brand new random() CSS function.

In its most basic form random() accepts a pair of comma-separated values that will act as the lower and upper bounds for the random value that will result, and an optional third value defining the step — the intervals between those limits. random( 0px, 10px ) will result in an arbitrary pixel value between 0 and 10, while random( 0px, 10px, 5px ) will result in 0, 5, or 10. Nothin' to it, at face value. transform: rotate( random( -2.5deg, 2.5deg ) ) suited my needs just fine, giving me a random rotation value between -2.5 and 2.5 degrees. By default this calculation is scoped to each individual element, which means that each note will have its own random rotation:

Choice of the word "scoped" there very deliberate, for reasons you'll soon understand.

.sidenote {
  transform: scale(0.925) rotate(random(-2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

Now we're talking — now those are some jaunty angles!

Quick work, though we're not quite done yet. For one thing, remember that I mentioned I was applying slightly different transforms to these components across breakpoints — overriding the transform property in a media query meant I needed to include that random rotation again, lest the new instance of transform undo my rotation altogether. Easy enough to fix:

.sidenote {
  transform: scale(0.925) rotate(random(-2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  .sidenote {
    /* Just using `transform: scale(1.1);` would override the rotation, so: */
    transform: scale(1) rotate(random(-2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

The result is that the baseline scale of my sidenotes changes while — notably — each element maintains the same random rotation across breakpoints, rather than being recalculated.

Of course, I'm using transform in my little timeline animation as well (in browsing contexts where animation-timeline: view() is supported, at least). By animating a transform that didn't include that rotate() value, my rotation could be once again be undone, and my sidenotes summarily de-jauntified.

I am a professional technical writer.

Just as easily fixed; I just needed to repeat the rotate transforms inside my @keyframes rule as well:

.sidenote {
  animation: movein ease-in-out;
  animation-timeline: view();
  /* … */
  transform: scale(0.925) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}
@keyframes movein {
  0%,
  100% {
    opacity: 0.5;
    transform: scale(0.925) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
  50% {
    opacity: 0.9;
    transform: scale(1) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

As before, no recalculation takes place in terms of each individual note's rotation inside or outside of the animation window — the reason being, all these calls to random() share the same random base value (or seed) used to generate the rendered value.

The base value is the randomly generated number that provides the basis for calculating the value that results from the call to random(). When random( 0px, 100px ) is called, a random seed between 0 and 1 is generated and used to perform the calculation of the resulting value - if the value of that seed is .5, the resulting value is 50px. If the value of the seed ends up being .25, the resulting value is 25px. Any two random() calculations based on the same seed will always give you the same end result.

The way I'm using random() in the snippet above, the rotation value that results from the first evaluated call to random() will be the value that results from the the other calls to random(), since they're all able to share the same base value used to generate that rendered value. Once random() is called and a base value is generated, an identifier that represents that seed value is created — a random cache key that can be used anywhere that cache key is in scope. In the examples you've seen so far here, the cache key is leaning on the default scoping behavior: scoped to individual elements (each instance of .sidenote), the property name (transform), and the index of that call — the order in which random() was called within the value of that property.

That's a lot on paper (and I found the concept of index scoping particularly tricky, I don't mind admitting), but it does make a lot more sense one we start putting some of this into practice. To start with, let's step through some of the random() usage you've already seen in a little more detail:

div {
  transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

The first call to random() generates a random seed between 0–1, uses it to calculate a value between -2.5deg and 2.5deg, and creates a cache key — an invisible identifier that represents the random seed. Here, that cache key will be scoped to the first random() value in subsequent transform declarations that are applied to each individual element targeted by the selector. Given these calls to random() using the same values, on the same element (any individual div), within the same property (transform), as the first call to random() in each declaration — that is, at the same index — the random seed already available to that scope is used for the calculation, and the same rotation results. If our page contains two divs, they'll both end up with different random values since the cache key is scoped to each individual element.

FYI

CSS is declarative, which means that there's no assumption of any specific evaluation order and "the first call to random" doesn't necessarily mean "the one at the top."

That's the detail that necessitates all the repetition, messy as it might seem: we couldn't have a shorthand that says "use the same value as that other random()" if "that other random()" may or may not have been evaluated yet. By repeating the values, these functionally-identical instances of random() can share a single base value regardless of their evaluation order.

Given another element altogether, we leave the scope where that cache key applies — so a new random seed is created to perform that calculation and a new cache key is generated for that new scope:

<div></div>
<div></div>
<p></p>

div {
  transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

p {
  transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

In this snippet three discrete cache keys are generated, each representing a different seed value, and each resulting in a different rendered value. One for each div, scoped to the transform property and and first index (the first instance of random() in the declaration). For each individual div on the page, and given the same transform property, a call to random() at the same index uses the same seed — each div ends up with a different rotation value, and those values are maintained across breakpoints. Naturally, that cache key is out of scope for the subsequent p, so a new value is calculated there.

FYI

Keep in mind that this is element-based, not selector-based — so long as we're targeting the same element, using the same property, and a value with the same index, the same cache key applies:

<div class="rightround"></div>

div {
  transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  .rightround {
    transform: rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

Different selector, but selector isn't a scoping factor — for the same element, using the same property, with the same random() index, the result is the same rotation.

Again, how random() works mechanically might seem a little arcane, but the out-of-the-box behavior gives us predictable results with relatively little code, and "keep the scoping as tight as possible" is an inarguably sensible default for any addition to the web platform. For my part, leaning on defaults means my little sidenotes play out something to the tune of:

Looking at you here, 1900s-era JavaScript.

:root {
  --scale-down: 0.925;
  --scale-up: 1;
}

.sidenote {
  align-self: flex-end;
  animation: movein ease-in-out;
  animation-timeline: view();
  /* … */
  transform: scale(var(--scale-down)) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  .sidenote {
    /* … */
    transform: scale(var(--scale-down)) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

@keyframes movein {
  0%,
  100% {
    opacity: 0.5;
    transform: scale(var(--scale-down)) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
  50% {
    opacity: 0.9;
    transform: scale(var(--scale-up)) rotate(random(2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

That's a lot of repetition, I know, but remember that there's no assumption of execution order in CSS — any one of these random() calls could be the one that defines their shared cache key.

Now, leaning on the default scoping behavior gets the job done for my little margin notes, but doesn't mean we're stuck with the default scoping behavior. So far we've only been passing random() a minimum and maximum value, but that first argument can instead be used to define a random key, with a specific identifier and specific scope — the second argument then defines the minimum value, and so on:

.sidenote {
  transform: rotate(random(--random-rotation auto, -5deg, 5deg, 1deg));
}

Used this way, that first argument will allow you to specify two things. The first is a dashed identifier (prefixed with --) that will act as the cache key. The second is a keyword that dictates whether that value should be scoped to a property (property-scoped) or property and index (property-index-scoped), to individual elements (element-scoped) or all matching elements identically, to individual elements and property and position (auto, the default), or a fixed number (fixed) which you'd likely only use for debugging purposes. Once we've established a random key and a scope where it applies, we can reuse it in other instances of random() — an explicit means of saying "if a random seed is already available in this scope, use it."

Mind the comma placement here, too — the dashed identifier and scope keyword make up one argument. I may or may not have tripped over rotate( random( --random-rotation, auto, 0px, 10px ) a few times myself.

Let's walk through our scoping options one at a time:

auto

In the example above, the --random-rotation identifier I specified just ends up serving as a human-readable representation of the cache key — by specifying auto for the scope, I'm still just leaning on the default per-element property and index scoping.

:root {
  --scale-down: 0.925;
  --scale-up: 1;
}

.sidenote {
  align-self: flex-end;
  animation: movein ease-in-out;
  animation-timeline: view();
  /* … */
  transform: scale(var(--scale-down)) rotate(random(--sidenote-rotation auto, 2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  .sidenote {
    /* … */
    transform: scale(var(--scale-down)) rotate(random(--sidenote-rotation auto, 2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

@keyframes movein {
  0%,
  100% {
    opacity: 0.5;
    transform: scale(var(--scale-down)) rotate(random(--sidenote-rotation auto, 2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
  50% {
    opacity: 0.9;
    transform: scale(var(--scale-up)) rotate(random(--sidenote-rotation auto, 2.5deg, 2.5deg));
  }
}

It adds a little more noise to an isolated case like this one, but I certainly wouldn't mind having a human-readable label for the availability of a given cache key if we assume a couple thousand lines of real-world CSS between these instances of random().

FYI

Despite sharing a shape, this identifier is very different from using random() in conjunction with a custom property. In this case, that property will still represent a call to the random() function itself, not the result of that function's evaluation:

:root {
  --random-margin: random(0px, 10px);
}

div {
  margin-block-start: var(--random-margin);
}

p {
  margin-block-start: var(--random-margin);
}

--random-size won't represent the results of calling random( 0px, 10px );, the way const randomSize = ${ Math.floor(Math.random() * 10 )px would — it represents a fresh call to random( 0px, 10px ) every time it's used.

My JavaScript-addled brain recoils in horror.

Again though, the addition of a manually-specified cache key doesn't gain us anything over using a generated cache key apart from a human-readable label for what are expected to be shared random() results, and specifying auto will result in the same scoping rules. What specifying a cache key does gain us is the ability to change the scope where that key will be available:

property-scoped

The invisibility of default/auto scoping has the potential for confusion once we start adding a little real-world complexity, particularly when it comes to the "index" part of the equation. Given the following, we might expect all these calls to make use of the same random key, same seed, and same rendered result:

div {
  margin-block: random(1rem, 5rem);
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    margin-block: random(1rem, 5rem) random(1rem, 5rem);
  }
}

Here, we're targeting the same element inside and outside the media query and we're using the same property, but the cache key generated by the first call to random() is scoped to the first random value of the margin-block declaration applied to each div — even though we might expect these declarations to give us the same rendered result, the declaration using the start and end shorthand will have an identical margin-block-start, but generate a new random value for the margin-block-end. If we wanted these declarations to be functionally equivalent, we need something a little outside of the default scoping rules.

If we instead specify property-scoped to say that the random key should be scoped to just the property — not the index — we can reuse that calculated value as both values in the margin-block shorthand:

div {
  margin-block: random(--random-margin property-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    margin-block: random(--random-margin property-scoped, 1rem, 5rem) random(--random-margin property-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
  }
}

Now the same value will be used for all three values.

We don't have to specify an identifier for the cache key. The previous snippet is functionally identical to:

div {
  margin-block: random(property-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
}

/* … */

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    margin-block: random(property-scoped, 1rem, 5rem) random(property-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
  }
}

Same result, but again: given a couple thousand lines of CSS between these statements, I'd just as soon know what random seed is meant to be associated with which declarations at-a-glance.

There's a catch here, though: by explicitly specifying property-scope, we've broadened the scope to only be limited by property — the cache key is no longer scoped to individual elements. Instead, any matching elements will be able to share a single cache key. If we were to only specify property-scope, like so:

.sidenote {
  transform: rotate(random(--random-key property-scoped, -2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

The resulting value will be shared by all elements matching our selector, across all properties — a result comparable to:

.sidenote {
  transform: rotate(/* Pick a random number between -2.5deg and 2.5deg */);
}

Good news, though: we can control that too.

element-scoped

By also adding element-scoped to this first argument, we can specify that the shared base value is scoped to individual elements and scoped to property only, not index:

.sidenote {
  transform: rotate(random(--random-key element-scoped property-scoped, -2.5deg, 2.5deg);
}

But the same way specifying only property-scoped meant "only scoped to property" and lost that individual-element scoping, we can broaden the scope to "individual elements, any property, any index" by specifying element-scoped alone:

div {
  margin-block: random(element-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    margin: random(element-scoped, 1rem, 5rem) 2rem;
  }
}

Here we're saying that per-element is the only applicable scope for this cache key — instead of the default/auto behavior of being scoped to individual elements, property, and index, this cache key is only scoped to individual elements. That means any instance of random() using these values in any property that applies to any div on the page can share the same random seed, and will result in the same value:

div {
  margin-block: random(element-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
}

@media (min-width: 55rem) {
  div {
    margin: random(element-scoped, 1rem, 5rem) 2rem;
  }

  div.by-class {
    padding: random(element-scoped, 1rem, 5rem);
  }
}

The resulting seed is scoped to each individual div in the rendered page, so all of these calls to random() will result in the same random value between 1em and 5em — but at higher breakpoints, any div.by-class will use that same value for padding as well.

Identifier Only

We can, in fact, go one step global-er. Specifying an identifier and omitting a specific scope for that identifier results in the broadest possible scope for a cache key: a random key not specific to property or index, and not scoped to individual elements — a random seed scoped to all elements and properties targeted by that styling.

“Global-er.” Professional technical writer, folks; can't stress that enough.

In this example, the same random seed will be used to calculate a random value that can be reused for any property and any index, but it won't be recalculated from one div to another, either. Unless otherwise overridden elsewhere, the same random value will be used across every div targeted by these selectors:

.sidenote {
  transform: scale(0.925) rotate(random(--random-key, -2.5deg, 2.5deg));
}

The resulting value will be shared by all elements matching our selector, across all properties — a result comparable to:

.sidenote {
  transform: scale(0.925) rotate(/* A random value between -2.5deg and 2.5deg */);
}

But because we're not scoping this to property or index, that means all of these calls to random() will result in the same value:

.sidenote {
  margin-block-start: random(--random-key, 1rem, 5rem);
}

@media (min-width: 30rem) {
  .sidenote {
    border: solid red;
    border-width: random(--random-key, 1rem, 5rem) random(--random-key, 1rem, 5rem) 0 0;
  }
}

@media (min-width: 50rem) {
  .sidenote {
    font-size: random(--random-key, 1rem, 5rem);
  }
}

Any property, any index — and because we've left the realm of auto or element-scoped, every .sidenote element will be rendered using the same random value for all of these properties, if and when they apply to the user's browsing context.

fixed

There's one more random key you can specify, and it's a weird one. Remember back where I said "when random( 0px, 100px ) is called, a random seed between 0 and 1 is generated to perform the calculation of the resulting value - how, given random( 0px, 100px ) and a random seed of .5, the resulting value would be 50px?" Well, the keyword fixed will allow you to specify a base value manually, using a number between zero and one — a hard-coded seed:

.sidenote {
  transform: rotate(random(fixed 0.5, -2.5deg, 2.5deg)); /* 0deg */
  transform: rotate(random(fixed 0.5, 0deg, 20deg)); /* 10deg */
  transform: rotate(random(fixed 0.25, 0deg, 100deg)); /* 25deg */
}

As you might have guessed, fixed has a pretty specific use case: it gives you a quick way to try out some of the values that might result from a call to random() without needing to scratch out the entire line and replace it with a static value. You'd never use this in production.

Odds are, you'll only reach for fixed when finessing the upper and lower bounds of a call to random() to see how a range of potential results would render — I certainly did, if only to try it out. Granted, trying a few different fixed values on for size was probably overkill for my purposes; realistically, a sense of how a whopping five (5) potential degrees of rotation will play across a few little side notes doesn't require much more than a couple of page-reloads and a little imagination. Still, tinkering with those base values does give you a little glimpse into the mechanics of how random() rolls the dice.

“Anything worth doing is worth—” well, you know the rest.

As for how those base values are shared between calls to random(), well, that clearly requires a little more imagination.

title: JavaScript for Everyone: New Game+
partialText:
We have great news. After months of effort, 3 new modules, 13 completely re-worked lessons and 20 new lessons (including practical exercises), JavaScript for Everyone's Updated content is now live!

Check it out!

We took feedback from the community about what they thought was missing from the course and overwhelmingly, people wanted practical exercises. It makes sense: JavaScript is a complex language to learn and there's not many better ways to cement new knowledge than by actually building with it.

Mat took this feedback as a challenge, formulated a plan and got to work, disappearing into a text editor and reappearing with pretty much a whole course's worth of new and updated material.

It's really inspiring to me, personally, because doing anything while it felt like our industry was being decimated felt impossible. Mat's resolve to keep doing what he does well: teach people, has been unmatched and the benefactors of that effort are everyone.

JavaScript for Everyone was already the canonical, high quality educational resource for learning JavaScript, but now, it's at a whole new level.

So what are you waiting for? Take it for a spin and truly understand how JavaScript works!

Check it out!
